paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder whose features overlap with those of Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Features include aortic aneurysm and dissection, mitral valve disease, hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity and kyphoscoliosis. Clinical variability is striking, both within and between families (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015). Some affected individuals have tall stature and others have growth retardation, low muscle mass and distal arthrogryposis (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Kuechler et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported a 9-year-old European American girl whose healthy parents were nonconsanguineous. At birth she had distal arthrogryposis, with contractures of the right hand (most severe in the 3rd and 4th fingers) and of all toes. She also had a midline facial nevus flammeus and mild hypotonia. She failed to thrive, and her gross motor development was delayed. At 17 months she had hypertelorism, prominent eyes, blue sclerae, a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate, retrognathia, mild pectus excavatum and pes planus. Her large joints were hyperextensible. Muscle bulk was reduced, with low tone and diminished reflexes, and subcutaneous fat was markedly reduced. She walked at 24 months with a waddling gait and a positive Gowers sign. Her neurocognitive development was normal. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. Growth retardation persisted, and at age 7 she weighed below the 1st centile. Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months showed no cardiac defect. Her aortic root dimensions were normal (z score 0.39 at age 6.5 years). A quadriceps biopsy at age 7 showed only mild focal type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse, with no dystrophic or inflammatory changes.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with an autosomal dominant disorder whose features overlapped with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Seven members aged 40 to 68 years had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three died of aortic dissection and rupture. Four had mitral valve abnormalities, ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation. Other features included subtle craniofacial changes (long face, high-arched palate, retrognathia), pectus deformity, scoliosis, velvety skin, varices and hiatal hernia. Autoimmune features included HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease and celiac disease.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) summarized 43 patients (23 male, 20 female) with TGFB3 mutations from 11 families. Their features overlapped with Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Four patients had type A dissection (median age 51 years) and 6 had type B dissection (median age 44.5 years). The authors observed no early dissection, no dissection at small aortic size, no striking arterial tortuosity and no ectopia lentis. Clinical variability was striking, both within and between families.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) studied a girl with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, hypertelorism, low muscle mass and growth retardation. Exome sequencing identified a heterozygous c.1226G-A transition in the TGFB3 gene, resulting in a cys409-to-tyr (C409Y) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutation had arisen de novo. The variant was not present in dbSNP130, the EVS database or 1000 Genomes. Cys409 is the penultimate cysteine of the cysteine knot and is conserved across TGF-beta family ligands. No mutations were found in TGFB2, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, FBN1 or FBN2. Secreted TGFB3 C409Y did not activate a TGF-beta reporter in cultured cells. In Xenopus embryos, coinjection of mutant and wildtype RNA at a 1:1 ratio reduced pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signals to about 40% and 60% of wildtype levels, respectively, consistent with a dominant-negative effect. The mutant had no effect on BMP/SMAD1 signaling. The authors concluded that the mutation is hypomorphic and that reduced TGF-beta signaling likely accounts for the phenotype.

The mutation had no effect on BMP/SMAD1 signaling, and the authors concluded that it is hypomorphic.

paragraphs.text: Kuechler et al. (2015) studied a father and his 2 children with tall stature, arachnodactyly, hyperextensible joints, hypertelorism and bifid uvula, without cardiac, aortic or eye involvement. In all 3, they identified a heterozygous c.898C-G mutation in the TGFB3 gene, predicting an arg300-to-gly (R300G) substitution. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and segregated with the phenotype. The authors suggested that Arg300 mutations presumably increase TGF-beta signaling.
